entries.title: Moving from up north to Florida — what should I know about the Pick 3 scene?

body.text: We may move near Tampa next spring, and Pick 3 is my little daily ritual. Florida players: what should I know? Midday and evening rhythms, where you like to check results, whether the Fireball add-on is worth the fun, anything a newcomer would not think to ask. I would love lived experience rather than the rulebook.

entries.title: Dreamed about fish again — grandma's book says 231

body.text: Three nights running I dreamed about fish. My grandmother's dream book puts fish at 231, and her handwriting in the margin says "play it a week." So 231 box it is, for a week. That is my whole method and I love it. What are your numbers telling you this month? This is my personal belief and my grandmother's book — I am not claiming it does anything but make me happy.
My mama's book says fish is money coming. Either way it is a sweet way to remember your grandma. WTG for keeping the tradition alive.
231 has a nice bounce to it. Adding it to my box list this week just for the company.
No dream number is more or less likely than any other — and honestly that is the nicest part. Play the memory, enjoy it, spend what it is worth to you and not a dollar past that.

summaryPoint.text: Dream numbers carry the same chance as any other combination; the value is the tradition, not the mathematics.

body.text: My aunt swears by her book too. Family tradition is half of why I play at all.
That is it exactly — it is about the people. The numbers are just how we hold them.

summaryPoint.text: For the believers in the thread, dream numbers are a way of carrying family memory, not a claim about outcomes.

body.text: This thread is why I love this place.

entries.title: Finally a decent box hit after two dry months (small but mine)

body.text: After two months of nothing, my 419 box finally came through last week — $290 on a fifty-cent ticket. I did a little dance at the kitchen counter. It is grocery money and a nice dinner, not a life change, but it made my whole week. No ticket photo — I never post barcodes or serials, and neither should you.

attachment.story: A regular box hit on a long-played family number, told first-hand. No ticket image was uploaded and no claim beyond the story itself is made.

body.text: WTG Pat!! The hits that end a dry spell are the sweetest ones.
Wonderful! 419 must mean something in your family — enjoy that dinner.
Congrats! The kitchen-counter dance is mandatory, I do not make the rules.
Congrats Pat. Also a model post — story told, no barcode, no serial number, no claim number. New folks, that is how you share a win.

entries.title: Scratch-off talk — what's in your wallet this week?

body.text: Scratch talk for August. I set myself a ten-dollar weekly ceiling and I stick to it — it keeps the hobby friendly. This week: one $5 crossword-style ticket and a $2 quick one. Broke even on the crossword. What is in your wallet, and what is your ceiling?
One $3 ticket with my Saturday coffee, that is my whole routine. Got a free-ticket result last week, which always feels like a holiday.
The crossword ones take me forever and I enjoy every minute. Ceiling here is $5 a week.
Break-even weeks are the honest average. A posted ceiling is the best system anyone in this thread runs, and I include mine in that.

summaryPoint.text: The thread's shared position: a fixed weekly spending ceiling is the habit that keeps scratch play a hobby.

body.text: I only buy one when the cashier is someone I like. It is a vibe purchase.
Vibe purchase is exactly right. Ten a week here too, and the ceiling holds even when the office pool is on.

entries.title: Powerball roll streaks — what's the longest run you've followed?

body.text: Every time Powerball goes on one of those long roll streaks, my office pool doubles and the group chat wakes up. What is the longest run you have personally followed, and did you buy more or sit tight? Also — I read the LotteryCorner piece on the 2015 matrix change and now I am curious: did that change really make long runs more common? Asking LotteryCorner Research to weigh in on that part.

researchReply.label: LotteryCorner Research
researchReply.questionResearched: Did the October 2015 Powerball matrix change make long jackpot runs more common?
whatWeFound: Yes, in the direction you would expect. On October 7, 2015, Powerball moved from 5-of-59 plus a Powerball of 35 to 5-of-69 plus a Powerball of 26. That lengthened the jackpot odds, so on average more drawings pass without a jackpot winner and prize runs last longer than under the older matrix.
Run length still varies a great deal: ticket sales rise as a prize grows, which raises the chance that someone somewhere matches on any given late-run drawing.
researchReply.whatRemainsUncertain: How any particular run ends — that depends on which tickets people actually buy, drawing by drawing.

body.text: I only buy in when the office does. Two tickets, that is my ceiling, win or lose.

Longest I tracked was a stretch back in 2021, on paper the whole way. The Research note above says it well — longer odds per drawing means more rolls on average before somebody hits, and no way to know how long any single run goes.

summaryPoint.text: The 2015 matrix change lengthened per-draw jackpot odds, which is why long roll streaks became more common on average.

body.text: I buy one ticket when a run gets long, mostly for the daydream. The dream is worth the two dollars to me.
Same here. The cash-versus-annuity arguments in the group chat are half the fun. There is a whole poll thread on that now.
Florida checking in — our pool at work does five dollars each when a run gets long. We have a written agreement now after one near-argument. Highly recommend the boring paperwork.

researchReply.label: LotteryCorner Research
researchReply.questionResearched: Do pair frequencies over a short window tell you anything about future Pick 4 draws?
whatWeFound: Each Pick 4 digit is drawn independently, so every ordered pair has the same chance on every drawing. Over a six-week window it is normal for a few pairs to appear several times and others not at all — that spread is what independent random draws look like, not a signal.
Tracking sheets are a well-loved part of daily-game culture and a fine way to organize play. They do not change what the machine draws.
evidence: Basic counting: one hundred equally likely digit pairs per position pairing
researchReply.whatRemainsUncertain: Nothing material — pair independence follows from the draw procedure itself.

body.text: My back pair 19 keeps me company most weeks. Nothing scientific — it is my mama's birthday.

Nice sheet. One thing worth saying out loud: over a couple of months, some pair always tops the list just by chance — a flat random draw still produces streaks. It does not mean the pair is special, and it is not a lean for the next draw.

summaryPoint.text: Some pair always tops a short-window tally purely by chance; a leader on the sheet says nothing about the next drawing.

body.text: I keep 23 and 32 both, whichever way the dream goes.
Y'all are organized. I just play quick picks and watch the big games.
Bill, that is exactly why I asked LotteryCorner Research to weigh in — their note is up top. Accepting your reply so newer players see it first.
WTG Bill, helpful as always.
Still playing my pairs either way. It is a ritual, not a strategy, and I am at peace with that.

entries.title: My Cash 3 sum-range filter — an entertainment system, not a promise

body.text: Posting my summer revision since a few folks asked in the monthly threads. Up front, as always: this is entertainment and organization, nothing more — no filter changes the odds of a fair draw. What it changes is how many combinations I have to look at, which is the part I enjoy. Structured fields below, walk-through table after.

Filter walk-through, one week

Step             Combos left
----             -----------
All straights    1000
Sum 9 to 18       ~660
Drop triples       650
My rotation          3

attachment.rules: Keep straights whose digit sum lands between 9 and 18, drop triples, then rotate three boxed picks per week from what is left.
attachment.example: Week of 7/6: kept 126, 345 and 780 (sums 9, 12 and 15), played each as a fifty-cent box.
attachment.assumptions: Assumes you enjoy the bookkeeping. The filter narrows how many combinations I look at; it does not change what the machine draws.
attachment.disclosure: This is a member method or historical research workflow. It does not guarantee future wins.

body.text: Love how tidy this is. I borrow the sum idea for my Pick 3 sheets.
You math folks amaze me. I will stick to birthdays, but WTG on the write-up.
Honest question — does running a filter like this actually win more over a year?

summaryPoint.text: A member asked whether the filter wins more over a year; the author's own answer is that it cannot and does not.

body.text: It does not, and I want to be plain about that: the odds are identical for every combination, filtered or not. What it wins me is time and tidiness. I keep a results sheet against my own picks for fun, and it lands where chance says it should.

summaryPoint.text: The author states plainly that the filter does not and cannot improve results; every combination carries identical odds.

body.text: I respect that you say that out loud, Bill.
Same. Systems as a hobby, not a promise — that is the spirit of this whole board.
